content: 1. Primaquine is a medication used in combination with other drugs to prevent and treat malaria caused by mosquito bites in regions where malaria is prevalent. 2. Malaria parasites enter the body through mosquito bites and reside in tissues such as red blood cells or the liver. 3. Primaquine is administered after other medications, like chloroquine, have eradicated the malaria parasites in red blood cells. It targets and eliminates parasites in other tissues, preventing the recurrence of infection. 4. Both primaquine and the initial medication are necessary for a complete cure. 5. The United States Centers for Disease Control (CDC) provides updated guidelines and travel recommendations for malaria prevention and treatment worldwide. 6. Primaquine should be taken orally as directed by your doctor, usually once daily. 7. It is recommended to take the medication with food to minimize stomach upset. 8. Follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Primaquine is typically taken for two weeks after leaving a malarious area. 9. It is initiated during the last 1–2 weeks of other malaria treatment or immediately after completing the initial treatment. 10. The dosage depends on the type of infection and your response to treatment. 11. Take this medication regularly and exactly as prescribed. Do not take more or less than directed. 12. Do not stop taking it before completing the treatment, even if you feel better, unless instructed by your doctor. 13. Prevent mosquito bites by using insect repellents, wearing protective clothing, staying in air-conditioned or screened areas, using mosquito nets, and applying insect-killing sprays. 14. Purchase insect repellents before traveling. The most effective repellents contain diethyltoluamide (DEET). 15. No drug treatment is entirely effective in preventing malaria. Seek medical attention immediately if you develop symptoms of malaria (e.g., fever, chills, headache, flu-like symptoms), especially while in a malarious area or even after completing this prescription. 16. Common side effects of primaquine include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, stomach upset, and abdominal cramps. 17. This medication is prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. 18. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare. 19. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for medical advice about side effects. 20. Before taking primaquine, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. 21. This product may contain inactive ingredients that can cause allergic reactions or other problems. 22. Primaquine may cause dizziness. Alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can exacerbate this effect. 23. Avoid driving, using machinery, or performing tasks requiring alertness until you can do so safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. 24. Primaquine may cause a condition affecting heart rhythm (QT prolongation). 25. The risk of QT prolongation may increase if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. 26. Low potassium or magnesium levels in the blood may also increase the risk of QT prolongation. 27. This risk may be heightened if you use certain drugs (e.g., diuretics or water pills) or have conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. 28. This medication must not be used during pregnancy as it may harm an unborn baby. 29. Women of childbearing age should undergo a pregnancy test before starting this medication. 30. It is crucial to prevent pregnancy during and after treatment with primaquine. 31. Both men and women must use reliable forms of birth control (e.g., condoms, birth control pills) during treatment. 32. Men should continue using birth control for at least three months after completing treatment. 33. Women should continue using birth control for at least one menstrual cycle after completing treatment. 34. If you become pregnant or suspect pregnancy, inform your doctor immediately. 35. Traveling to a malaria-endemic area during pregnancy significantly increases the risk of death and complications for both the mother and the infant. 36. The CDC recommends continuing other malaria treatments (e.g., chloroquine) throughout pregnancy to prevent harm to the unborn baby (e.g., hemolytic anemia). 37. After delivery, primaquine treatment may be completed. 38. It is unknown if this drug passes into breast milk. 39. The doctor should test your infant for G6PD deficiency before breastfeeding. 40. Drug interactions may alter the effectiveness of your medications or increase the risk of serious side effects. 41. Keep a list of all products you use (including prescription/nonprescription drugs and herbal products) and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. 42. In case of overdose with serious symptoms (e.g., passing out or trouble breathing), call 911. Otherwise, contact a poison control center immediately. 43. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. 44. Laboratory and/or medical tests (e.g., G6PD blood test, blood cell counts) should be performed before starting this medication and during treatment. 45. Keep all medical and lab appointments. 46. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of the next dose, skip the missed dose. Take your next dose at the regular time. 47. Store this medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. 48. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. 49. This information is a summary and does not contain all possible details about this product. 50. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs.
